results.summary:
`hkb heartbeat` is now a compare-and-swap on the lock ref: an empty commit made locally with `commit-tree`, pushed with a `--force-with-lease` refspec on `refs/kb/locks/<n>/<k>`. The lease is the whole check, so a dispatcher reclaim (which deletes the ref) rejects the push atomically and hkb exits 3 LOCK_LOST.

`<expected>` is the worker's own record — the local mirror of the ref, or the new `lock_sha` field the dispatcher writes on the attempt row — never a fresh read of the ref, which would stomp whoever holds it. A warm worker beats with zero API calls: no task read, no run-record read, no write.

Only a rejected lease may stop a worker. It is verified once against `GET git/ref/...` (gone = LOCK_LOST; still ours = the local chain drifted, so resync and beat again); every other git failure is classified 'unavailable' and falls back to the run-comment heartbeat with a note on stderr. Profiles pick the path with `"heartbeat": "auto"|"ref"|"comment"` in board.json; cloud tiers that cannot push refs use `comment`.

The dispatcher reads the lock ref's committer date before reclaiming a stale-looking attempt, since a CAS beat leaves no trace in the run comment. Its existing `listLocks` call is hoisted to serve both that and the orphan sweep, and the commit is read only for an attempt that already looks stale.

If you touch this: the design rests on `classifyLeasePush` never returning 'lost' for anything but a rejected lease. A false LOCK_LOST kills a healthy worker; a missed one only wastes work the dispatcher discards — so ambiguity always funnels into the authoritative ref read.

Two things the next worker should know. (1) The worker permission policy (DENY_PATTERNS in src/model.js) blocks the lease-push command from a worker's Bash on purpose — hkb runs it from its own child_process, and SKILL.md now tells workers never to push the ref themselves. (2) That same pattern is matched against the whole Bash command string, so a worker whose `hkb complete --summary "..."` merely *mentions* the command is refused permission to finish. I hit this and had to use `--summary-file`. It is a protocol foot-gun worth fixing: match the deny pattern against the command being run, not against text passed as an argument to another program.
